body:
This seems a little unfortunate that the syntax is this delicate, I understand we're trying to force people to think about what behaviour they want but this may be too far.

I see multiple problems defining it like this:

- At-a-glance valid values might not be valid. For example I don't think this fully expands on what (otherwise seemingly valid) values like `"toolbar nowrap wrap"` or `"listobx block inline"`) mean. Are they entirely invalid? That would be sad. 
- In addition I think it's too much to expect some attributes to be positional and others not. 
- For completely invalid syntaxes (i.e. `"wrap"` - no behaviour specified), I wonder if "defaulting `none`" would be too aggressive?
- I also worry about how we might extend this in the future, let's say for arguments sake we add a new value of `menulist`, how can developers use the new value and have it gracefully degrade? They'd need to be able to express something like `"menulist menubar"` so that old browsers fall back to `menubar` and new browsers pick up `menulist`. Likewise for adding new modifiers.

Ultimately I think it should operate conceptually more like a set of bitflags: we scan the token list for the first keyword and that is what sets the bit; subsequent groups (e.g. behaviour, memory|nomemory) are simply ignored.

We should try to do our best to have a consistent semantic/heuristic that expresses developer intent, but that is still flexible enough for when developers get it wrong. We can't throw on invariants, so we instead we should try to make the most of the given input.

This should be a `DOMTokenList`; it will make it much easier for developers to use (it has `add`/`remove`/`toggle`/`replace`), and importantly it has `supports`, which will allow us to potentially extend the focusgroup tokens while allowing developers to feature detect new tokens.

E.g. I can imagine some code like `focusGroup.replace('radiogroup', 'none')` or so - could be quite ergonomic.

+
    +

  1. Entering from before: Pressing Tab focuses "Bold" + (has focusgroupstart, taking precedence + over order-modified document + order).

    2. + +

  2. After arrow navigation to "Italic": Pressing Tab + to leave and then Shift+Tab to return focuses "Italic" (memory of last + focused item takes precedence over focusgroupstart).

    3. +

Key Conflict Elements
+ +

A key conflict element is an element that has native (built-in) arrow key behavior + that conflicts with Directional Navigation, and either:

+
    +

  • is a focus group item; or

    • + +

  • is the currently focused area of a top-level traversable's DOM + anchor and is a focusable area within a focus group + scope.

    • +
+ +

Which elements have such behavior, and on which axes, is determined by the user agent based + on the element's built-in arrow key behavior.

+ +
+

Examples of elements that are typically key conflict elements include:

+ +
    +
  • input elements (most, but not all types use arrow keys)
    • +
  • textarea elements
    • +
  • select elements when the arrow-key axis used by the + focusgroup is the same axis used by the select element
    • +
  • Elements with the contenteditable attribute
    • +
  • Focusable scrollable regions, when the scroll direction is in + the same axis as the focus group
    • +
  • audio and video elements with visible controls
    • +
  • iframe and object elements with focusable content inside
    • +
+
+ +

A key conflict element that is itself a focus group item can be + reached via Directional Navigation. (Other key + conflict elements, such as those with tabindex="-1", + are not reachable via Directional Navigation, but the user can still focus them + through other means such as programmatic focus or pointer interaction.) However, once a + key conflict element has focus, its native behavior takes precedence and + Directional Navigation does not occur.

+ +

To allow users to escape a key conflict element via + sequential focus navigation, all focus group + items in the same focus group scope as the currently focused area of + a top-level traversable's DOM anchor participate in sequential focus + navigation while that focused element is a key conflict element. Forward + sequential navigation moves focus to the next sequentially focusable element in + order-modified document order, and backward sequential navigation moves focus to + the previous one. Elements that are not focus group items + of the same focus group — including those inside opted-out subtrees — are not skipped during + this navigation. If no further sequentially focusable element exists in the + navigation direction, sequential navigation proceeds normally beyond the focus group.

+ +

On most desktop platforms, sequential focus navigation is + triggered by Tab (forward) and Shift+Tab (backward). On other + platforms (such as TV remotes or game controllers), the user agent determines the + appropriate input for sequential navigation.

+ +

This override applies only when the DOM anchor of the currently + focused area of a top-level traversable is the key conflict element + itself. When focus is on a focusable area whose + DOM anchor is a descendant of the key conflict element (such as + a control within a video element's user-agent shadow tree), the override does + not apply, and normal sequential focus navigation applies within the + element's internal controls.
